title: Chirag Paswan hits back at Rahul Gandhi’s caste discrimination remarks
author: Amarnath Tewary
content_html:
In response to Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s recent remarks on caste discrimination, Union Minister of Food Processing Industries and Lok Janshakti Party (Ram Vilas) leader Chirag Paswan on Saturday (August 29, 2026) demanded that those who were in power before the BJP regime should explain why discrimination against Dalits still persists in society.

Mr. Paswan was speaking on Congress leader Rahul Gandhi’s recent remarks on the purification ritual at a venue in Uttarakhand where party president Mallikarjun Kharge had addressed a gathering at Haldwani’s Ramlila ground on August 8, 2026. Mr. Gandhi, on Saturday, asked Prime Minister Narendra Modi to “file an FIR against those who conducted the purification ritual”. He said that what was done there was equivalent to “untouchability” and that Dalits across the country face such incidents.

Meanwhile, he also demanded the resignation of Hindustani Awam Morcha (Secular) leader, Santosh Kumar Suman from the Bihar Cabinet after the party, an NDA ally, sought a review of the reservation policy and sub-categorisation of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

Mr. Suman and his father, Union Minister of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Jitan Ram Manjhi, both on Saturday, however, asked for Mr. Paswan’s resignation first and asked him to “properly understand” what they had said earlier on the issue of reservation that had triggered rift among ruling NDA allies.

Mr. Paswan, while speaking to media persons, strongly defended caste-based reservation, calling it an “unyielding constitutional right rather than charity”.

While saying further that reservation remains fully necessary because caste-based discrimination and social inequalities have not disappeared from modern society, Mr. Paswan asserted that “reservation, gifted by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar in the Constitution, cannot be abolished or undermined by any power on earth because groups or protesters demand it”. “If discrimination continued in society despite this, it implies that they (who ruled the country for long) too, failed to strengthen the foundations effectively”, he said.

Defending the constitutional basis for reservation, Mr. Paswan added that “it stems from social discrimination and untouchability, not economic criteria”. “Those who seeks change in its basis, must change the Constitution”.

Mr. Paswan further said, “he (Mr. Suman) should resign first (from the Cabinet) before demanding this”. “The basis of reservation was social discrimination and it should not be viewed from an economic perspective... discussing it from an economic perspective goes against the Constitution”, reiterated the Union Minister.

Mr. Suman responded to Mr. Paswan on Saturday in a post on social media handle X, “as far as the issue of my resignation, I’m ready for this, but my younger brother (Chirag Paswan) should start this by resigning first. My younger brother should understand better that I had never ever spoken about the creamy-layer, neither had talked about ending the reservation but, of sub-categorisation in reservation regime and both should not be mixed to confuse people… .” His father Jitan Ram Manjhi in Gaya on Saturday too defended what he had said earlier.

“He (Chirag Paswan) should resign first, and then we all will follow him… he must understand properly what Santosh Suman had said…”. “Those who have been left behind in society should get the benefits of reservation as the time has changed… it's time for Gen-Z and people’s aspiration”, Mr. Suman added while speaking to presspersons.

title: Maharashtra government in touch with 338 of the 404 stranded in Nepal
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
Maharashtra government is in touch with 338 of the 404 people stranded in Nepal after the flash floods and mudslides, the government said on Saturday (August 29, 2026).

Follow the Nepal flash floods LIVE

Of them, 41 returned from Saga on Saturday (August 29) evening, while 106 tourists will reach Nagpur at 4.30 a.m. on Sunday (August 30). 45 tourists who had travelled with an Ahilyanagar-based travel agency have also entered India. “About 143 citizens are on their way to return to the state successfully,” the Maharashtra government said in a statement issued on Saturday night. Till 31 August, a total of 69 tourists are expected to land in Mumbai.

“We are in touch with a few individuals of the groups of stranded tourists. One-to-one touch has not yet been possible. We are collating the list of individuals,” an official told The Hindu on Saturday (August 29) night.

“Government agencies at various levels are working round the clock to help the citizens of Maharashtra and tourists who had gone for religious tourism,” an official said.

The government has started helplines for the people stranded in Nepal. The Nagpur-based tourists have started their journey from Bihar towards Nagpur. The group of 45 tourists travelling with an Ahilyanagar-based agency were in Chitwan during the flood. “Since the route to Kathmandu is closed today, they are being brought via Lumbini in Nepal, and after reaching Ayodhya today, further planning will be done as per the instructions of the government,” the official said.

The government is trying to establish contact with eight persons from Mumbai, who are yet to be traced. “Information has been given about eight tourists from Borivali and Andheri. They are stranded in Nepal due to the disaster. Out of these, efforts are being made to get more information from Lakshminarayan Acharya from Andheri, but as he or others in the group cannot be contacted through mobile, there are difficulties at present. Efforts are being made to establish contact with them. The administration is in touch with the relatives of these tourists in Mumbai,” the government said.

“The Ministry of External Affairs has sent a list of 149 Indian tourists who have safely entered Nepal from China till the end of August 28 to the states. Action is being taken to safely reach them in their districts. Instructions have been given to the concerned citizens of the districts of Maharashtra to verify and collect their information and names. These tourists will return to India soon. In this, the Emergency Control Room (BMC EOC) of the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) has not received any call regarding any citizen of Mumbai city or Mumbai suburban districts so far,” the government added.

title: In a notable address in New York City, RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat stated that true Hindutva does not exclude Muslims from Bharat, asserting that any Hindu who believes otherwise ceases to be a Hindu
author: Ishita Mishra
content_html:
Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat on Saturday (August 29, 2026) said that Hindutva does not envisage a Bharat (name he uses for India) without Muslims, asserting that a person who believes Muslims should have no place in the country would cease to be a Hindu.

Addressing an event in New York City where he spoke with leaders from different communities and religions, Mr. Bhagwat said that Muslims, during a dialogue with him, had questioned him about the RSS’s vision of a “Hindu Rashtra” and whether Muslims would be driven out of the country. “I said, no, that is not Hindutva. If any Hindu thinks that there should be no Muslims in Bharat, he will not remain Hindu,” he said.

Mr. Bhagwat stressed that while people may follow different religions, humanity remains one. “We live in a society where religions may be different, but humanity is one,” he said, adding that india’s tradition had been to provide shelter to people irrespective of their religious identity.

He also cited the RSS’s service activities to underline his claim that the organisation does not discriminate on the basis of religion. According to him, around 1.3 lakh service projects are being run by RSS volunteers with the help of society.

Recalling an incident in Dadri, Haryana, where two aircraft from Muslim-majority countries collided, Mr. Bhagwat said RSS volunteers were among the first to reach the site. As all passengers had died, the volunteers helped arrange funerals and assisted relatives in identifying the victims, he said.

“We don’t have the thought that they are Muslims,” Mr. Bhagwat said, referring to the RSS volunteers’ approach to relief and service.

He said the organisation’s approach was rooted in the belief that “we” and “ours” should replace the narrow focus on “me” and “mine”. “Where there is ‘me’ and ‘mine,’ there is no solution. ‘We’ and ‘ours’ is the solution,” he said.

Mr. Bhagwat also referred to the RSS’s dialogue with members of minority communities, saying that the organisation had begun engaging more extensively with Muslims and Christians in Bharat after 2018. “Dialogue is the first step, and service is another step,” he said.

Invoking the example of Ramakrishna Paramahamsa, the RSS chief said the spiritual teacher had practised different religious traditions, including Islam and Christianity. He quoted him as saying: “As many ways, as many thoughts. All lead to one way.”

Mr. Bhagwat said the idea of the unity of humanity was embedded in India’s traditional thought as well as in the Constitution. He argued that social change could not be achieved through politics alone and called for local initiatives based on selfless service, dialogue and unity.

‘Things cannot be achieved through politics alone. Sorry to say, but the fact is that politics has now become a game of self-interest. Our experience in India is that we have to start with society, and we have started it,’ he said.

title: BJP says 'no caste angle' in Haldwani incident, accuses Rahul Gandhi of playing divisive politics
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Saturday (August 29, 2026) cited testimonies of two Scheduled Caste eyewitnesses to claim that they exposed Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi’s narrative over an alleged incident in Haldwani, Uttarakhand, earlier this month.

The attack came after Mr. Gandhi targeted the party and the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), alleging that a “purification” ceremony was organised at a rally venue addressed by Congress chief Mallikarjun Kharge in Haldwani. Mr. Gandhi also sought a First Information Report (FIR) on the incident.

At a joint press conference, BJP leaders Guru Prakash Paswan and Sudhanshu Trivedi argued that a 20-day delay in raising the matter and seeking an FIR suggested that there was no genuine issue or legal basis. They said the matter was being used by the Congress as a “political opportunity” to further its politics of creating “social divisions”.

They played videos of two eyewitnesses, who are members of an organisation that cleaned the stage and organised a “havan” at the venue, which is a Ramlila site. They denied allegations of caste discrimination.

Referring to the eyewitnesses, Mr. Trivedi suggested that a counter-FIR could potentially be filed without specifying against whom.

Accusing Mr. Gandhi of continuously supporting “forces that break society” and trying to create “a narrative based on lies”, Mr. Paswan described him and the Congress as “anti-Dalit” and “neo-feudal”. He said the party and its leaders had ill-treated Mr. Kharge, former Puducherry Chief Minister V. Narayanasamy, and senior Haryana Congress leader Kumari Selja, among others.

“History is witness to how Babasaheb Ambedkar and Babu Jagjivan Ram were treated. Babu Jagjivan Ram had to leave the Congress, and for the first time the country saw a person from the Dalit community become Deputy Prime Minister, in a government formed by the Bharatiya Jana Sangh,” Mr. Paswan said. He alleged that Karnataka Deputy Chief Minister G. Parameshwara had publicly said he was not made Chief Minister because he was a Dalit.

“Today your government is in many States. How many SC, ST, and OBC Chief Ministers are there?” he asked, listing leaders from the Scheduled Tribe (ST) and Scheduled Caste (SC) communities who have held important positions under BJP-led governments, including President Droupadi Murmu, Union Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal, besides several Chief Ministers and Deputy Chief Ministers.

“Who ensured that Babasaheb Ambedkar would not win the election? From Babu Jagjivan Ram to Babasaheb Ambedkar, Kanshi Ram and Sitaram Kesri, what kind of treatment was meted out to them? And they ask us about our commitment... the history of the Congress is one of neo-feudalism, extreme casteism, and being anti-Dalit,” Mr. Paswan said.

Mr. Trivedi alleged that Mr. Gandhi and the Congress repeatedly raise different identity issues, including gender, region, State, language and caste, with what he described as the underlying agenda of making “Hindus fight among themselves”. He also alleged that the Congress had a record of neglecting or mistreating Dalits.

The BJP leader mentioned cases of violence against Dalits in Rajasthan and Karnataka under the Congress governments to allege that the party failed to protect them.

title: Congress chief Kharge must get justice, we demand FIR: Rahul Gandhi on rally venue ‘purification’ in Uttarakhand
author: Sandeep Phukan
content_html:
Mounting a sharp attack on the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) over the alleged shuddhikaran (purification) ceremony at the venue of a rally addressed by Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge in Haldwani earlier in August, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi, on Saturday (August 29, 2026), said the act amounted to the practice of untouchability, which is a crime under the Constitution.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi must ensure that a First Information Report (FIR) is registered against those responsible, Mr. Gandhi said, accusing the BJP-RSS of seeking to prevent Dalits from progressing and living with dignity and respect.

“We are demanding justice for the Congress president. Give the Congress president justice in Uttarakhand. It is the duty of the Central and State governments to ensure that Kharge ji gets justice,” Mr. Gandhi said at a press conference here.

He declined to take questions on the controversy surrounding Penguin Random House India and the publication of Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson Sonia Gandhi’s memoir, Belonging, calling it a “digression strategy”.

Penguin India reportedly dropped plans to publish the memoir after Ms. Gandhi refused to remove passages critical of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the RSS, and China’s alleged occupation of Indian territory.

“I don’t have any interest in this right now; I am interested in what they have done to Kharge ji,” Mr. Gandhi said.

Nearly 20 days had passed since the alleged incident, but no action had been taken, he said. Referring to Uttarakhand BJP president Mahendra Bhatt’s reported defence of the ceremony, Mr. Gandhi said the State BJP leadership had effectively justified an act of untouchability.

“We demand that an FIR be lodged against those who have done this. PM Modi states that he belongs to every caste and is the Prime Minister of the country, but his party chief of Uttarakhand defends shuddhikaran,” he said.

Opening his presentation with images of the Constitution and the Manusmriti, Mr. Gandhi framed the controversy as part of a larger ideological conflict between the constitutional values associated with B.R. Ambedkar, Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru, and the ideology represented by the BJP-RSS.

His invocation of the Constitution and the Manusmriti came amid the BJP’s recent attempt to portray him as “anti-Hindu”, accusing him of selectively attacking Hindu religious texts while remaining silent on religious texts of other faiths during the Congress’s recent ‘Chhatron ki Goonj’ (echo of students) programme in Pune.

Caste discrimination and untouchability continued to be a reality despite being prohibited by the Constitution, Mr. Gandhi said, citing instances of Dalit children allegedly being made to clean toilets in schools, discriminatory practices in public spaces, and violence against Dalit grooms.

“The more successful the Dalit person is, the more fierce the attack on him or her is,” he said, referring to similar alleged instances involving Mr. Kharge, Rajasthan Congress leader Tikaram Jully, and Union Minister Jitan Ram Manjhi.

“This is another name for untouchability. The BJP people practise untouchability. When they do shuddhikaran, they say that Dalits cannot touch, as they are impure,” Mr. Gandhi said.

The alleged ceremony was performed at Haldwani’s Ramlila Maidan on August 10, 2026, two days after Mr. Kharge addressed a Congress gathering there. Mr. Kharge subsequently raised the issue in Parliament, demanding action under laws dealing with untouchability.

Mr. Bhatt had reportedly maintained that the venue had been polluted by slogans inappropriate for a religious place, prompting the Congress to accuse him of justifying the ritual. The Uttarakhand Congress unit has alleged that the Shri Ram Sena performed the ceremony and had links with the BJP, a charge denied by the ruling party.

Mr. Kharge had also raised the issue at the recent Congress Working Committee meeting and expressed anguish over what he said was inadequate support from certain quarters within the party.

Clarifying Mr. Kharge’s remarks, Mr. Gandhi rejected the suggestion that the Congress president had complained of receiving little support from the party as a whole.

“That’s not actually what happened. He said certain people didn’t support him. He didn’t in any way say that the vast majority of Congress did not support him. I supported him, and a whole number of other people supported him,” Mr. Gandhi said.

In the Rajya Sabha, Leader of the House and Union Minister J.P. Nadda had said the BJP did not subscribe to such activities and that the incident would be investigated.

Nearly 20 days had passed since the alleged incident, but no action had been taken, he said. Referring to Uttarakhand BJP president Mahendra Bhatt’s reported defence of the ceremony, Mr. Gandhi said the State BJP leadership had effectively justified an act of untouchability.
“We demand that an FIR be lodged against those who have done this. PM Modi states that he belongs to every caste and is the Prime Minister of the country, but his party chief of Uttarakhand defends
shuddhikaran
,” he said.
Opening his presentation with images of the Constitution and the
Manusmriti
, Mr. Gandhi framed the controversy as part of a larger ideological conflict between the constitutional values associated with B.R. Ambedkar, Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru, and the ideology represented by the BJP-RSS.
His invocation of the Constitution and the
Manusmriti
came amid the BJP’s recent attempt to portray him as “anti-Hindu”, accusing him of selectively attacking Hindu religious texts while remaining silent on religious texts of other faiths during the Congress’s recent
‘Chhatron ki Goonj’
(echo of students) programme in Pune.
Caste discrimination and untouchability continued to be a reality despite being prohibited by the Constitution, Mr. Gandhi said, citing instances of Dalit children allegedly being made to clean toilets in schools, discriminatory practices in public spaces, and violence against Dalit grooms.
“The more successful the Dalit person is, the more fierce the attack on him or her is,” he said, referring to similar alleged instances involving Mr. Kharge, Rajasthan Congress leader Tikaram Jully, and Union Minister Jitan Ram Manjhi.
“This is another name for untouchability. The BJP people practise untouchability. When they do
shuddhikaran
, they say that Dalits cannot touch, as they are impure,” Mr. Gandhi said.
The alleged ceremony was performed at Haldwani’s Ramlila Maidan on August 10, 2026, two days after Mr. Kharge addressed a Congress gathering there. Mr. Kharge subsequently raised the issue in Parliament, demanding action under laws dealing with untouchability.
Mr. Bhatt had reportedly maintained that the venue had been polluted by slogans inappropriate for a religious place, prompting the Congress to accuse him of justifying the ritual. The Uttarakhand Congress unit has alleged that the Shri Ram Sena performed the ceremony and had links with the BJP, a charge denied by the ruling party.
Mr. Kharge had also raised the issue at the recent Congress Working Committee meeting and expressed anguish over what he said was inadequate support from certain quarters within the party.
Clarifying Mr. Kharge’s remarks, Mr. Gandhi rejected the suggestion that the Congress president had complained of receiving little support from the party as a whole.
“That’s not actually what happened. He said certain people didn’t support him. He didn’t in any way say that the vast majority of Congress did not support him. I supported him, and a whole number of other people supported him,” Mr. Gandhi said.
In the Rajya Sabha, Leader of the House and Union Minister J.P. Nadda had said the BJP did not subscribe to such activities and that the incident would be investigated.

title: Choosing compassion over catch
author: Navamy Sudhish
content_html:
It was supposed to be a regular fishing day off the coast of Malappuram, but as Abdul Salam and his crew hauled their ring net, they noticed it refused to rise properly. Submerged below the surface was a rare sight -- a massive whale shark entangled in the meshes.

Recognising the endangered creature, the fishers immediately launched a delicate two-hour operation, carefully untangling the giant by cutting open the net and guiding it back into open waters. That selfless act marked the first recorded rescue and release of a whale shark in Kerala — a story now chronicled alongside dozens of others in ‘Guardians of the Gentle Giants: A Tribute to Kerala’s Whale Shark Rescuers’, a new book published by the Wildlife Trust of India (WTI).

Authored by Jithin Jose alongside a team of six others, the book documents 54 successful rescue operations conducted by Keralam’s fishing community since 2017. The publication serves as a tribute to coastal communities whose quick thinking and compassion have given the world’s largest fish a vital lifeline. In another incident off the coast of Thiruvananthapuram, fisher Mohammad Maheen and his crew spent over three hours freeing a whale shark from a shore seine net. “When we first tried to control the net, three of my crew members were injured. My priority was keeping my men safe while making sure we didn’t cause any more harm to the shark,” Maheen recalls.

Conservation project

Once hunted extensively along the Indian coastline, the whale shark (Rhincodon typus) faced a perilous future until WTI launched the Whale Shark Conservation Project across Keralam and Lakshadweep in 2017. Moving beyond simple awareness drives, the project established a holistic model engaging fishers, harbour management committees, schools, local self-governments and State departments.

“Over 200 training sessions have been conducted to educate local communities on the biology of these gentle giants — which are cold-blooded, Schedule I protected fish under India’s Wildlife Protection Act. The book also doubles as a practical guide, featuring a standing response manual that details immediate reporting steps and emergency protocols during entanglements,” says Jithin Jose.

Choosing to rescue a trapped whale shark demands immense economic sacrifice from fishing families dependent on daily catches. To safely release the animals, fishers often have to cut open their nets. “Cutting open a net often costs fishers a full day’s catch, and fixing the resulting damage means losing several working days. Releasing a whale shark takes more than just knowing it is protected; it requires real courage, deep empathy, and a willingness to put the creature’s survival above personal financial gain,” explains Sajan John, marine projects head of WTI.

While WTI currently offers ₹25,000 as a reward, this amount falls short of covering total losses, prompting ongoing efforts to secure additional financial relief from the State government. “It is the quiet, everyday decisions of local communities—like fishers choosing to cut their nets to save a helpless creature—that turn abstract environmental goals into meaningful action. Ensuring fair and prompt compensation for damaged nets is essential to protect fishers’ livelihoods and ensure they can afford to keep saving these endangered giants,” he adds.

title: Illegal trekking, ‘hidden spot’ tourism raise alarm in Karnataka's Western Ghats
author: Darshan Devaiah B.P.
content_html:
Residents and environmentalists across the Western Ghats, particularly in Kodagu and Chikkamagaluru districts, have raised concerns over the growing trend of private groups and tour operators promoting hidden and remote natural spots for commercial trekking and adventure activities.

Locals fear that the sudden influx of tourists in ecologically fragile areas could cause irreversible damage to forests, water sources, and wildlife habitats.

Residents allege that several travel agents and private groups, particularly from Bengaluru and Mysuru, are identifying lesser-known hills, waterfalls, and other natural locations and promoting them on social media. Treks are subsequently being organised to these spots without permission from the Forest Department.

The increased footfall has resulted in tourists leaving behind plastic waste and other garbage, they alleged.

In Kodagu, the Forest Department recently intensified action against unauthorised commercial trekking in sensitive forest areas and warned travel agents and tour operators against promoting illegal trekking routes.

The warning followed the circulation of social media videos showing trekking activities to mountains, waterfalls, and areas where Strobilanthes kunthiana, popularly known as Neelakurinji, an endemic shrub seen in the Western Ghats, is in bloom at Perur village near Napoklu. The department said that social media posts are being used to promote commercial mass trekking in sensitive areas around Nelji, Perur, and the neighbouring regions.

“Over the past few days, we have been seeing several illegal tour operators arranging treks and taking tourists to hidden spots in the hills without permission. The main concern is that several lesser-known places inside and around forest areas are now being exposed to tourists for commercial purposes,” Thimmaiah K.B., resident of Nelji, told The Hindu.

He said that the area has several small waterfalls and other natural spots that are increasingly being accessed by tourists. Many of these locations are located in or close to sensitive forest areas and are not equipped to handle large numbers of visitors.

“With the Neelakurunji in bloom, more people are coming here. If the visitors are allowed to enter these places without restrictions, they could damage the plants and other vegetation. Such activities can also disturb wildlife and increase the possibility of human-wildlife conflict. We are worried that continued unregulated tourism will severely affect the fragile ecosystem,” he said.

Another resident, Biddappa of Marandoda in Madikeri taluk, said his village was facing a similar problem at a place locally known as Baliyatre, where a small waterfall is located on a hill.

He said that Baliyatre was never intended to be a tourist destination and, more importantly, the water source is vital for the villagers. “The water from this area is an important drinking water source for the people of Marandoda. It is a place that needs to be protected and not converted into a tourist spot,” Mr. Biddappa told The Hindu.

“People are promoting the location on social media, making reels, bringing tourists and organising treks for commercial purposes. Visitors have already started leaving garbage and polluting the area, putting our drinking-water source and the surrounding forest at risk,” he added.

Chikkamagaluru sees similar trend

A similar trend has emerged in Chikkamagaluru, where environmentalists have urged the district administration and the Forest Department to prohibit private groups from conducting adventure and sports activities in forest areas without permission.

Recently, private groups organised off-road activities in parts of Kalasa and Koppa. Following objections from local groups, the Forest Department intervened and stopped the activity in Kalasa. However, environmentalists said similar activities continued in the Koppa region.

Activist Nagaraj Koove said that environmentalists had studied the impact of such activities on the fragile Malnad ecosystem. “The impact was huge and such activities could cause serious damage. In the name of sports activities or exploring the Malnad region, private organisations are conducting such events with profit as the primary objective. They offer participants a sense of adventure and thrill, but the environmental cost is borne by the forests and local communities,” he told The Hindu.

“Forest areas are not playgrounds for private commercial events. Such activities, particularly those involving vehicles and large groups, should be stopped unless they are properly regulated and permitted by the authorities,” he added.

The risks were highlighted recently when a group of tourists allegedly drove a vehicle to the edge of a nearly 3,000-ft.-deep gorge at the Rani Jhari viewpoint in Mudigere taluk. The visitors were reportedly at the spot to shoot videos/reels for social media. Kalasa Range forest officials seized the vehicle and registered a case against the group.

Meanwhile, Forest Minister Ramalinga Reddy, who was in Kodagu on August 28 for a departmental meeting, said that he had received complaints from residents regarding unauthorised trekking and tourist activities in forest areas and had instructed officials to take action against those conducting trekking activities illegally in forest areas.

“Forest areas cannot be opened up for commercial activities merely because some locations become popular on social media. If such activities are allowed unchecked, they can disturb wildlife and affect the ecological balance. Officials have been directed to identify such activities and take action against tour operators and private groups violating the rules,” he added.

(With inputs from Sathish G.T.)

title: Chennai’s second airport: grounded until take-off
author: Sunitha Sekar
content_html:
Nearly three decades after the idea to build a second airport for Chennai was first mooted, the Tamil Nadu government finds itself at the drawing board again, hunting for a fresh site, after the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) government cancelled the Parandur airport project.

Cheyyur and Gummidipoondi were among the 11 locations originally considered when the search for the second airport project began nearly seven to eight years ago. At the moment, it is not clear why these two locations had never made it to the shortlist of four sites — Parandur, Pannur, Thiruporur, and Padalam. Though discussions had been held on Pannur too, it is not clear if it is still in the race.

Also Read | Dropping Parandur airport project an irreversible setback for Tamil Nadu: M.K. Stalin

Cheyyur airspace under IAF

Sources say that if the Cheyyur site is pursued, the State government may have to get the approval of the Ministry of Defence since the site could fall within the airspace controlled by the Indian Air Force, Tambaram. At Gummidipoondi, the Pulicat Lake is closer to the site, and it remains to be seen how bird movement will or will not affect air traffic. “No decision has yet been taken on the site. The State government will take a decision soon,” a source says. It is learnt that a site inspection is expected to happen anytime.

After finalising the site, the government must request the Airports Authority of India (AAI) to do the pre-feasibility study and give its recommendation. Subsequently, roping in a consultant and applying for the site clearance will start afresh.

After the Sriperumbudur airport project proposed in the mid-2000s was aborted, Parandur came the closest to hosting Chennai’s second airport. Now, all the procedures for building a second airport must begin from scratch.

For the second airport project planned at Parandur in Kancheepuram district on 5,846 acres, the government had completed the acquisition of 1,802 acres, which Industries Minister Keerthana said would be used for industrial purposes.

Enhancing capacity at Meenambakkam

Since building an airport at any chosen site will take a minimum of five to seven years, the State government has shifted its immediate focus to enhancing the capacity of the existing airport at Meenambakkam by constructing T5 Terminal (near the remote bays and between the main and secondary runways). With the completion of phase 2 modernisation (building of T2 and T3 Terminals), the airport’s capacity will increase to 35 million passengers a year and the handling capacity will further be expanded to 55 million passengers a year on the completion of T5 Terminal. An elevated corridor from National Highway 32 needs to be constructed to enable air passengers to enter T5 Terminal.

But air passengers and aviation experts say a few projects being carried out by the AAI are already reeling under delays. For instance, phase 2 modernisation’s original deadline was 2022. But it is yet to be completed.

Constructing the elevated corridor and the terminal will take years, an aviation expert says. He points out that a detailed project report needs to be prepared for T5 Terminal and the elevated corridor. “To fix the designs, call for bids, and then complete the entire process, it could take a minimum of five years, provided the AAI meets all the deadlines and the project is carried out at a meticulous pace,” he adds.

Sandhya Vedullapalli, a frequent flyer, says she has encountered a few issues at the Chennai airport. “It is painful to walk to the multi-level car park to board the cab. For years together, they have been modernising the airport and building an integrated terminal, and this is putting so many people to inconvenience. It is not easy to push the trolley and walk outside the airport since it is not a smooth contiguous path,” she adds.

Be it the state of washrooms or the number of dining and shopping options, everything is so much better at the Bengaluru and Hyderabad airports, Ms. Vedullapalli says, adding that if the second airport had been built at Sriperumbudur by now, air passengers wouldn’t be suffering. “There should be policy continuity. One government proposes it, then another drops it. Until another airport is built, it is the air passengers who will have to put up with various issues, and it is unfair,” she adds.

The government should soon find a site to address the development needs of the city even while balancing the environmental concerns.

Direct flights gone to Bengaluru

A. Sankar, another frequent flyer, says Chennai has lost out on adding direct flights to many destinations, while Bengaluru seems to have grabbed them in time. Earlier, there were direct flights to Paris and Tokyo, but they are no longer available from Chennai. Meanwhile, Bengaluru now boasts direct flights to Tokyo, Paris, Amsterdam, Vietnam, and the Maldives. “Chennai really needs direct flights to many European destinations, and initiatives have to be taken,” he adds.

Industry leaders have reiterated the need for state-of-the-art airport infrastructure as it will not only help in drawing more airlines and connecting the city directly to more domestic and international destinations but will also drive up the economy. The ‘Aerotropolis’ model, which is fast emerging now, revolves around airport-led development wherein businesses, commercial complexes, residential communities, and the logistics industry come up in the airport’s vicinity. Ravichandran Purushothaman, chairman of Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) Southern Region, summed it up rather well: “An airport is far more than a piece of transport infrastructure; for a capital city and economic powerhouse like Chennai, it is a strategic enabler of economic growth, global competitiveness, trade, tourism, investment, and job creation.”

The CII notes in a statement that while modernising the Meenambakkam airport is essential, it is only a medium-term plan for the city. “Choosing a site [for the second airport] quickly is critical and once it is done, the project should be expedited and executed with urgency to ensure Chennai retains its competitive advantage among India’s leading industrial and investment destinations.”

‘A costly mistake’

Vijay Gopalan, former chief financial officer of AirAsia India, says the decision to scrap the Parandur airport project will prove to be a costly mistake, pushing Chennai’s growth behind by at least 10 years. While the government claims that an airport alone will not decide investments, what it fails to acknowledge is that such decisions reflect poorly on a city’s image, he says. “The perceptions matter so much when you have to attract young talent. While I’m glad the government is finally waking up to the need for setting up more Global Capability Centres (GCCs) for young talent and delegates to choose the city, we need better social infrastructure, and of course a good airport. A world-class airport substantially boosts the image of a city and its branding. The faster we understand this, the better it is for the city. Else, we will stagnate while Bengaluru and Hyderabad grow at a phenomenal pace,” he says.

Chennai’s primary competitive advantage lies in its robust manufacturing ecosystem, which continues to attract substantial global investments into Tamil Nadu, says Dinesh K. Krishnan, national treasurer, The Air Cargo Agents Association of India. “However, the current handling of air cargo fails to match this industrial momentum, falling significantly short of the operational efficiency delivered by privately managed airports in Bengaluru and Hyderabad,” he says.

 

‘Improve utilisation’

There is also an argument in a few quarters on whether Tamil Nadu needs a new international airport. Uvakai Research Foundation, in its recent report, says there is scope to improve the utilisation of the existing airport before going in for another major airport. But aviation experts point out that unless a newly built second airport run by a private operator is established, Chennai’s aircraft and cargo movement cannot increase significantly. From the third position in passenger traffic, Chennai has been pushed to the fifth spot. “The Bengaluru and Hyderabad airports are growing remarkably because of their efficiency,” an expert says.

Mr. Krishnan adds that today, trade logistics face severe operational bottlenecks, and exporters and freight agents frequently complete customs clearance in Chennai, only to transport their cargo by bonded trucks to the Bengaluru airport. “This detour is driven by Bengaluru’s faster cargo processing, lower air freight rates, and overall operational predictability,” he adds. With professionalised terminal management, the Chennai cargo facility can effectively service regional trade for another 10 to 15 years, while long-term second-airport plans materialise, he says.

Industry leaders have reiterated the need for state-of-the-art airport infrastructure as it will not only help in drawing more airlines and connecting the city directly to more domestic and international destinations but will also drive up the economy. The ‘Aerotropolis’ model, which is fast emerging now, revolves around airport-led development wherein businesses, commercial complexes, residential communities, and the logistics industry come up in the airport’s vicinity. Ravichandran Purushothaman, chairman of Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) Southern Region, summed it up rather well: “An airport is far more than a piece of transport infrastructure; for a capital city and economic powerhouse like Chennai, it is a strategic enabler of economic growth, global competitiveness, trade, tourism, investment, and job creation.”
The CII notes in a statement that while modernising the Meenambakkam airport is essential, it is only a medium-term plan for the city. “Choosing a site [for the second airport] quickly is critical and once it is done, the project should be expedited and executed with urgency to ensure Chennai retains its competitive advantage among India’s leading industrial and investment destinations.”
‘A costly mistake’
Vijay Gopalan, former chief financial officer of AirAsia India, says the decision to scrap the Parandur airport project will prove to be a costly mistake, pushing Chennai’s growth behind by at least 10 years. While the government claims that an airport alone will not decide investments, what it fails to acknowledge is that such decisions reflect poorly on a city’s image, he says. “The perceptions matter so much when you have to attract young talent. While I’m glad the government is finally waking up to the need for setting up more Global Capability Centres (GCCs) for young talent and delegates to choose the city, we need better social infrastructure, and of course a good airport. A world-class airport substantially boosts the image of a city and its branding. The faster we understand this, the better it is for the city. Else, we will stagnate while Bengaluru and Hyderabad grow at a phenomenal pace,” he says.
Chennai’s primary competitive advantage lies in its robust manufacturing ecosystem, which continues to attract substantial global investments into Tamil Nadu, says Dinesh K. Krishnan, national treasurer, The Air Cargo Agents Association of India. “However, the current handling of air cargo fails to match this industrial momentum, falling significantly short of the operational efficiency delivered by privately managed airports in Bengaluru and Hyderabad,” he says.
‘Improve utilisation’
There is also an argument in a few quarters on whether Tamil Nadu needs a new international airport. Uvakai Research Foundation, in its recent report, says there is scope to improve the utilisation of the existing airport before going in for another major airport. But aviation experts point out that unless a newly built second airport run by a private operator is established, Chennai’s aircraft and cargo movement cannot increase significantly. From the third position in passenger traffic, Chennai has been pushed to the fifth spot. “The Bengaluru and Hyderabad airports are growing remarkably because of their efficiency,” an expert says.
Mr. Krishnan adds that today, trade logistics face severe operational bottlenecks, and exporters and freight agents frequently complete customs clearance in Chennai, only to transport their cargo by bonded trucks to the Bengaluru airport. “This detour is driven by Bengaluru’s faster cargo processing, lower air freight rates, and overall operational predictability,” he adds. With professionalised terminal management, the Chennai cargo facility can effectively service regional trade for another 10 to 15 years, while long-term second-airport plans materialise, he says.
